Objectives: Controlling and preventing the spread of halogeton, increasing productivity of the unit, and stabilizing the range.
Planned_Implementation:
Generally the seeding shall be performed by use of acceptable commercial-type grain drills. If, in the opinion of the officer in charge, the soils are too loose or the area is too trashy to obtain satisfactory seeding by use of drills, he may authorize the use of acceptable commercial-type fertilizer spreaders, power broadcasters or other suitable broadcast seeding equipment. Also, should the plowing operations be completed at a time unfavorable to the seeding operations, the officer in charge may require the seeding to performed as a separate operation at a more favorable time. In either case the method and time of seeding shall be determined by the officer in charge. Any and all seeding equipment used must be supported by adequate hoppers, agitators, and controls to satisfactorily plant seed at a uniform rate and at an average depth of one-half inch to one inch.

Seedbeds shall be solid seeded except for omission of rock outcrops, deep washes, or steep slopes as determined by the officer in charge. When drills are used, drill rows shall not be less than twelve nor more than fourteen inches apart, When required by the officer in charge the contractor shall provide for one man to ride the seeding equipment to insure the seed is being properly distributed and covered.

The rate of seeding shall be approximately six pounds per acre.

The seed for the most part will be Crested Wheatgrass seed seeded at the approximate rate of five pound per acre with the understanding that sufficient Alfalfa seed may be added to form a mixture if determined advisable by the officer in charge which will thereby increase the rate of seeding to approximately six pounds per acre.

Seed at the rate per acre specified will be furnished by the Government.

The contractor shall be responsible for the delivery of the seed to the project site from the Government warehouse located in Burley, Idaho and for the protection of the seed from theft and weather while en route to, and from, and at the project site. Unused seed at the project site at the time of completion or termination of the contract shall be returned to the Government warehouse by the contractor. All empty seed sacks will be caved and returned to the Government warehouse

Objectives:
The objective of this
treatment is to establish a desirable perennial plant community that would help achieve a healthy,
functioning rangeland and significantly reduce the potential for spread of invasive annual grasses
and noxious weeds. High wildfire intensity removed the majority of existing plant cover making the
burn area more susceptible to expansion of annual exotics.
Planned_Implementation:
Following the Glyphosate spray in the spring, the treatment area outside of the Great Rift and Bear
Den WSAs would be drill seeded. The proposed drill
seeding area is approximately 14,967 acres. A standard rangeland drill and rubber tired tractor
would be utilized for the seeding treatment.
Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of drill seeding approximately 12,692 acres out of a 16,395 acre area
within the Bear Den Butte fire. Unburned islands of grass and sagebrush, numerous areas of rock, and areas of archeological
sites were the reason for reduction in acres completed. Seed was applied in dry conditions at the
beginning to wet ground later in the process. The contractor for the project was Richard Barney of Shoshone, Idaho. Nine rangeland drills
were used. The seed was premixed by ESR Staff with the assistance of fire crew. The project
was started on August 25, 2008 and completed on October 17, 2008.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY09 Monitoring Results
The drill seeding was completed in the fall of2008. Preliminary qualitative and quantitative
monitoring showed fair to good germination of seeded species. There was also good recovery of
existing native vegetation. The cool and wet June produced a germination of annual exotic
vegetation across the drill seeded area. Tumble mustard and prickly lettuce were the primary germinating annual species. It is expected that these annual species will be reduced in cover
over the next 2 growing seasons as perennial vegetation becomes more dominant.

Objectives:
The objective of this treatment is to reestablish a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches the
structural and species composition and diversity of the native plant community to help achieve a
healthy, functioning rangeland. Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of sagebrush is important to
maintaining the value of the area as sage grouse breeding and wintering habitat. Sagebrush is also
an important component of suitable habitat for a number of sensitive sagebrush obligate species.
The wildfire intensity impacted existing sagebrush cover which would not recover naturally without
providing additional seed source.
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 19,000 acres would be aerial seeded with a mixture of basin big sagebrush and\r\nWyoming big sagebrush in the winter of 2008/2009 (FY09). This area is the drill seed treatment\r\narea. This 19,000 acre area would be strip seeded.
Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of aerial seeding 9,500 acres out of an area of 19,050 acres. Rate of
application was approximately 1.00 pounds bulk seed per acre. The seed consisted of 4,760
pounds of Wyoming and 4,760 pounds of Basin Sagebrush which was mixed during the loading
process. The seed was applied to snow covered ground in strips from east to west. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding,
ID. Pilots for the seeding were Rod Thomas and Dale Thomas. The project was completed
using one helicopter and two sling type buckets. The project was started on 12/17/08 and
completed 12/18/2008.

Contract Cost: $ 28,500.00 
Seed Cost: $ 42,697.20
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results FY09
Qualitative and quantitative monitoring was established in FY09. No sagebrush seedlings were
documented in quantitative plots. Qualitative observations did not document seedlings. The
cool wet weather in June produced heavy cover of herbaceous cover which made observation of
sagebrush seedlings difficult. Monitoring will be continued in FY10.
Monitoring Results FY10
Qualitative and quantitative monitoring documented establishment of sagebrush seedlings in
FYI0. Sagebrush seedlings were documented in quantitative plots at .08 plants per square meter
across all plots. Qualitative observations did reveal some establishment of seedlings in small
patches across the treatment area. The cool wet weather in June produced heavy cover of annual
and perennial herbaceous cover which made observation of sagebrush seedlings difficult.

performed so drill furrows are perpendicular to the prevailing winds, that is, generally north and south.

competition for available nutrients and water. The seedlings would have a better chance of becoming
established under conditions of less competition.

This contract consisted of drill seeding 6064 acres. The contractor was responsible for furnishing labor, equipment, supplies, and material except for Government-furnished property
which consisted of nine rangeland drills and three drill
carts. Seed mixture was also provided by the Government. The
contractor was Diamond Back Construction, P.O. Box 791, Middleton,

consisting of Thomas N. Thompson, William E. Young, Charles

Doty and Wendy York. Contractor had also been awarded Black Ridge
#2 and Black Ridge #3, drill seeding contracts that bordered the
Black Ridge #1 contract. Contractor was given permission to work
all drills together from all three jobs. Contractor was sometimes
working a total of 21 drills behind seven tractors at a time. The
project was started 10 / 21/92 and completed 11/27/92. Most seed was
applied to bare ground.

The seed mixture consisted of:
Whitmar Bluebunch                           1.00 lb./acre
Secar Snake River                                1.00 lb./acre
Critana Thickspike                               0.75 lb./acre
Siberian Crested Wheat                    0.75 lb./acre
Alkar Tall Wheatgrass                        0.50 lb./acre
Boziosky Russian Wildrye                0.50 lb./acre
Eski Sainfoin                                          2.00 lb./acre
Appar Lewis Flax                                  0.25 lb./acre
Fourwing Saltbush*                            0.50 lb./acre

per drill. The remaining seed was pre-mixed.

Rate of Application: 7.25 lb./acre

Average Depth of Seed: One Inch

Project inspectors for the project were Scott Uhrig and Randall
Jayo. The Contracting Officers Representative was Bernie Jansen.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
1997:
•	Overall we were impressed by the recovery of the sites from recent fires.
•	It seemed like a remarkably cool summer with an unusually long growing season. We experienced some high heat and drying in August, but May and June were cold and July relatively cool in comparison to past summers.
•	There seemed to be a difference in the vigor of the Machaeranthera (hoary aster) between the control and other treatments. It was much more robust (more stems, bigger plant size, likely more flowers) in the control treatments at all the WSA and Potter sites.
•	At sites other than Ro, the native bunchgrass recorded during the cover study was Poa 90% of y
the time, with Stipa, Sitanian hvstrix, and basin wild re comprising most of the remainder.
•	It appears that the amount of flax seed could be reduced in future seedings that may occur in the area as it has become well established and is vigorously reproducing. Datasheets can be found in the project monitoring folder.

community would inhibit the expansion of annual vegetation and noxious weeds and restore key

Actual_Implementation: Bitterbrush seed was purchased. Inventories for cultural resources were performed by contract.\r\nThis drill seeding was conducted in the Dry pasture of the Dempsey allotment. Twin Falls District fire employees conducted the drill seed work.\r\nBitterbrush seed drilling began on 10/06/2011 and completed on 11/08/2011. Approximately 3,500 acres were drill seeded with bitterbrush. Six BLM rangeland drills were used. Seed was applied in dry condition to moist conditions. Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Results
Quantitative objectives identified for drill and aerial seeding are:
• For drill seed areas – establish seeded grasses at densities of 4 plants/m2 and seeded forbs at 0.5 plants/m2.
• For sagebrush aerial seed areas – 0.10 plants/m2.
• The amount of bare mineral soil (i.e. soil lacking cover of plants, litter, or biological soil crust) is within 10% of what would be expected for the site based on an adjacent unburned site or the ecological site description.
Qualitative objectives identified for drill and aerial seeding are:
• The majority of desired herbaceous perennial plants are producing seed.
• The plants must also have developed root systems that are extensive enough to provide soil stabilization and prevent uprooting when grazed, especially when soils are moist.

FY12
There were 24 monitoring plots established during the summer of 2012. Cover, density, and belt transect data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1, 2 and 3). Cover and density across the plots was dominated by cheatgrass. Percent cover of cheatgrass was moderate at 11.94. Seeded species detected in density plots included bitterbrush (.006/m2), bottlebrush squirreltail (.58/m2), flax (.006/m2), penstemon (.01/m2), sainfoin 9.03/m2), Siberian wheatgrass (.14/m2), yarrow (.08/m2) and Sandberg’s bluegrass (3.22/m2). Qualitative observations by fire ecologists revealed that fair germination of seeded species occurred in early spring. The latter part of spring was dry reducing growth and vigor of germinating plants. Summer was hot and dry. Competition from annual vegetation is currently moderate with the drill seeded species. No big sagebrush seedlings were detected in cover, density or belt transects.
FY13
The 24 monitoring plots were read during the summer of 2013. Cover, density, and belt transect data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1, 2 and 3). Cover and density across the plots was dominated by cheatgrass though slightly less in 2013. Density of seeded and other dominant species decreased slightly in 2013 probably due to extreme drought conditions. Belt transects across the bitterbrush drill seed area were documenting bitterbrush at .04 plants/m2. Qualitative observations revealed that seeded species were maintaining establishment for the previous year but drought was negatively affecting vigor and spring growth.
FY14
The 24 monitoring plots were read during the summer of 2014. Cover, density, and belt transect data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1, 2 and 3). Cover and density of cheatgrass decreased across the plots in 2014. Density of seeded and other dominant species increased slightly in 2014 probably due to decreased competition from annual species. Belt transects across the bitterbrush drill seed area were documenting bitterbrush at .04 plants/m2.
Qualitative observations revealed that seeded species were maintaining establishment from the previous year but drought was negatively affecting vigor and spring growth. Northerly exposures were maintaining good cover of seeded species. Southerly exposures were more scattered. It was evident that cheatgrass cover is less than the previous year due to drought conditions.

This project consisted of drill seeding 1,636 acres within the Bray
Lake Fire. Seed was applied in dry to conditions starting on the
south end and working north. An area designated to be harrowed
and broadcast seeded, due to lightly burned sagebrush, was drill
seeded after it was determined there wouldn’t be any issues with
tire problems. This was done with a different seed mix than the rest
of the area. The drill seeding area was to be 1,236 acres and the
harrowing area was to be 400 acres. Six rangeland drills were used.
Please see the attached map for the project location. The project
was completed by Twin Falls District Fire Crew. The seed was
premixed by ESR Staff and Fire Crew. The project was started on
October 22, 2013 and completed on October 31, 2013.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The drill seed treatment would be considered successful if:
The seeded grass, forb, and shrub species reach densities of:
1) 3 plants per square meter for grasses;
2) 0.3 plants per square meter for forbs; and
3) 0.10 plants per square meter for shrubs (bitterbrush).

FY 14
Siberian wheatgrass and big bluegrass were the only drill seeded plant species documented in the
density and cover plots. Sagebrush seedlings were documented in belt transects at 5 plants/ m\xb2.

FY 15
Establishment of seeded species was excellent in 2015. The abundant spring moisture increased
vegetation growth and vigor. Establishment of big sagebrush was still good and meeting
objectives.

FY 16
The establishment of drill seeded species continued to be excellent in 2016. The abundant spring
moisture in May increased vegetation growth and vigor. Establishment of seeded perennial
grasses and big sagebrush were meeting objectives. Cheatgrass remains in the plant community
but is scattered in the community.

PART 9-RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
FY 14
Siberian wheatgrass and big bluegrass were the only drill seeded plant species documented in the
density and cover plots. Sagebrush seedlings were documented in belt transects at 5 plants/ m\xb2.
The dry spring and summer months appear to have affected the establishment of other seeded
species. Noxious weed control and fence repairs were completed in 2014. Noxious weed
monitoring and control efforts will continue in 2015. The livestock grazing closure will continue
in 2015.
FY 15
Abundant spring moisture in 2015 substantially increased the growth and vigor of seeded
species. Qualitative observations reveal good establishment of seeded species including big
sagebrush and yarrow. Annual vegetation is still a component of the plant community but it is
expected to be less dominant in the future. Weed control was implemented and completed in
2015. Monitoring and control of noxious weeds will continue in FY16.

FY 16
Abundant spring moisture in May increased the growth and vigor of seeded species across the
treated area. Objectives have been met for the drill seeded grasses and sagebrush. Qualitative
observations reveal that overall the seeding has established well. Cheatgrass and medusahead
wildrye still remain in the plant community. It is recommended that spraying of a pre-emergent
herbicide to reduce annual vegetation cover be considered. The treated area has been placed into
the normal grazing rotation for the allotment.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
Rationale:  Establishment of a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches the structural, species composition and diversity of the indigenous native plant community would help achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland, significantly reduce the potential for spread of invasive annual grasses and noxious weeds, and substantially diminish and control soil erosion affects across the watershed.

Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of native grasses, forbs and sagebrush is important to maintaining the value of the area as mule deer winter range, sage grouse breeding and wintering habitat.  Native seed mixtures are also an important component of suitable habitat for a number of Sensitive sagebrush obligate species.

Seed Mix #2:
The purpose of this seed mix is the same as above except that the seed mix is more conducive and better suited for the environmental and soil characteristics (range sites) encountered in this part of the burn.

The purpose of this seed mix is to restore and recover as quickly as possible some of the more sandier soil areas in the northern portion of the burn with a very adaptive, drought hardy and good diversity native and non-native plants that will replenish and refurbish deteriorating rangeland areas where many older rangeland seedings have occurred and some native vegetation sites have lost their sustainability, been depleted in composition and productive due to droughts, insects, grazing and other fires in the past, and lost much of their essential soil stability capabilities as perennial plants have weaken over time and, in some instances, have been gradually replaced with annual weed forms such as cheatgrass, bur buttercup and mustards.  If weather conditions are favorable for the next few years, the seeding of this mixture will provide a persistent and sustaining ground cover for the protection and benefit of the soils and the watershed, and improve habitat and food source conditions for wildlife and livestock.

Sandberg bluegrass and sand dropseed are both native, perennial grasses that are known to occur in these sandy sites and do well in this particular precipitation zone.  Both should do well here.  The non-native Siberian wheatgrass is particularly favored in this area because of it ability to compete with the higher levels of cheatgrass found here.  Also it has a very successful germination and survival rate compared to other species here, especially some natives, it is very drought tolerant, and it is has good soil binding and stability qualities.  Although alfalfa is the only proposed forb, it purpose it aid as a nitrogen fixer in the soil for the benefit of other plants of the area, plus it provides a good ground cover and forage for wildlife and livestock.

Objectives:
The purpose of this project is to re-establish a perennial plant community in an area that has been invaded by annual
grasses and to allow recovery of the perennial vegetation that burned in the Cold Springs fire. The emergency fire
stabilization and rehabilitation project (ESR) will reduce the risk of invasion of annual grass, restore wildlife habitat,
and allow for recovery of native and previously seeded vegetation.
Actual_Implementation: The aerial seeding was done by Thomas Helicopters on 2/18/2002. The ground conditions were moist and frozen\r\nwith no snow. The project was inspected by Jeff Swanstrum and Clif Hall.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
The ESR plan for this fire lists three treatment objectives:

Livestock grazing may resume once post fire ground cover reaches 80-90 percent of pre fire levels. Perennial key species must qualitatively look vigorous and 50-60 percent of plants producing seed heads. Seeded species must have a sufficient root system to withstand being uprooted during grazing. In the late spring 2003 the mean canopy cover for the three sites within the drill seeded portion of the burn was 12.3 percent.  The composition of this cover was: 1.6% perennial grasses, 10.6% annual grasses, and 0.1% annual forbs.  The mean soil surface cover for the three drill seeded sites was 14.1%.  The composition was 1.8% perennial grasses, 8.8% annual grasses, and 3.5% litter.  The mean density for those perennial grass species present in the drill seeded portion of the burn were: Sandberg Bluegrass (Poa sandbergii) at 0.72 plants/m2 and Crested Wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum) 0.03 plants/m2.  The canopy cover for that transect within the portion of the burn not drill seeded was 7.6%.  The composition was 2.4% perennial grasses and 5.2% annual grasses.  The soil surface cover for that transect within the portion of the burn not drill seeded was 54.5%.  The composition was 18.2% perennial grasses, 18.2% annual grasses, 3% forbs, and 15.1% litter.  Sandberg Bluegrass and Crested Wheatgrass were present along that transect within the portion of the burn that was not drill seeded at densities of 1.3 plants/m2 and 3.2 plants m2, respectively.  No live shrubs were noted along any density transect in either portion of the burn. 

In 2002 the mean canopy cover for the three sites within the drill seeded portion of the burn was 15.3 percent.  The composition was: 1.2% perennial grasses, 3.0% annual grasses, and 11.3% annual forbs.  The mean soil surface cover for the drill seeded sites was 27.8%.  The composition was 0.3% annual grasses, 5.5% annual forbs, 14.7% litter, and 7.3% rock/gravel.  Point intercept cover for that transect within the portion of the burn not drill seeded was 70%.  The composition was 20% grass, 6.7% forbs, 10% cryptogamic crust, 16.7% litter, and 16.7% rock/gravel.  No live shrubs were noted along any density transect in either portion of the burn.

Soil surface cover for the unburned reference site was 40%.  The composition of the surface cover was: 1% perennial grass, 1.5% annual grass, 16.8% annual forbs, 1.3% cryptogamic crust, 14.7% litter, and 4.7% rock/gravel.  Point intercept cover for the reference site was 60%.  The composition was 10% grass, 16.7% forbs, 3.3% live shrubs, 26.6% litter, and 3.3% rock/gravel.

The cover data collected within the drill seeded area shows that the percentage of canopy cover and soil surface cover afforded by annual grasses increased from 3% to 10.6% and 0.3% to 8.8%, respectively, from 2002 to 2003.  This suggests that Cheatgrass, the predominant annual grass occurring within the boundaries of this rehabilitation project, is increasing at fairly rapid rate.

Data collected in 2003 from the monitoring site within the portion of the burn that was not drill seeded shows the density for Crested Wheatgrass was 3.2 plants/m2 along the transect.  The Crested Wheatgrass population present in this portion of the burn in resulted from seeding that occurred prior to the Cold Springs Fire.
Approximate 763 acres of the burned area was not drill seeded either because the acreage was in accessible to mechanized equipment or prior to the Cold Springs Fire the acreage supported a robust healthy stand of perennial grasses that would recover naturally if allowed to rest grazing for several growing seasons.  Over the past two growing seasons the pre-fire stand of Crested Wheatgrass located in the southwest corner of the burn and Sandberg Bluegrass stand located in the northeast portion have reestablished themselves very nicely.  The individual plants within these areas are quite healthy and robust in appearance and all have produced seedheads.

In the late spring of 2003 the drill furrows were still visible throughout the 198 acre portion of the burn that was drill seeded in the fall of 2001.  However, no evidence of seedling emergence/establishment was found.  The few Crested Wheatgrass and Sandburg Bluegrass plants encountered within this portion of the burn had regrown from old crowns that existed prior to the fire.  This portion of the project will afford little in the way of grazing value unless further effort is made to establish a new stand of perennial plants.  Additionally, a thorough survey of the entire burn yielded no evidence to indicate any establishment Wyoming Big Sagebrush and Alfalfa resulting from the aerial seeding that occurred in February 2002.

Continued monitoring of this fire site is not recommended unless additional rehabilitation efforts are initiated on the 198 acre portion that was drill seeded in the late fall of 2001.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Monitoring Method: In June 2007, 2 monitoring plots were established and recorded and 1 shrub-hoop transects was conducted.  Monitoring recorded plant species occurrence and cover, using Photo Point, Density, Gap Intercept, and Line-point Intercept methods. In 2008, Ecosystem Management Inc. was contracted and conducted the monitoring of the 2 established plots in July.  Aerial Seeding Density Monitoring/Evaluation was conducted in June 2008 by BLM personnel.  In 2009, a field review of the aerial seeding treatment area and was conducted by BLM personnel. 
Results:  In 2007, monitoring indicated the treatment was ineffective in re-establishing either a shrub or forb component within the plant community.  No shrubs, whether seeded or not, or no seeded forbs were recorded or observed.
In 2008, no aerial species recorded or observed at the site.  Although, cheatgrass and annual mustard were the dominant species, natural recovery of native POSE was good, 4.0/m\xb2.   Monitoring to date indicates the treatment was ineffective and was consider unsuccessful at that point in time.
In 2009, a field review of the aerial seeding treatment area was conducted and very few aerial seeded species were noted and the treatment was considered as being unsuccessful.  The post-fire vegetation: eastern extent of the fire primarily cheatgrass and some Sandberg bluegrass; the more central plateau area pre-fire scattered rabbitbrush with an understory of cheatgrass and Sandberg bluegrass; western plateau area predominated by cheatgrass. Post-fire vegetation of the steep rocky areas, which occupied a considerable area within the fire boundary, is characterized cheatgrass and mixed with native perennials. Recommendations:  The original plan for this area was to control the cheatgrass with an herbicide application followed by a drill seeding treatment of perennial grasses.  This seedbed situation would have been much more favorable to an aerial seeding treatment and would have provided a higher chance of success.

Objectives: Objective of this treatment is to establish plants in a density that will stabilize the soils on site in the short and long term, be competitive against invasive grasses/forbs and noxious weeds, provide a functioning ecosystem and critical forge and cover for sagegrouse and be resilient for livestock grazing.
Planned_Implementation: A total of 27,169 acres of drill seeding are proposed under the Emergency Stabilization Plan to protect and/or reestablish endangered springsnails, threatened bull trout, candidate sage-grouse habitats, and the habitat for several sensitive species. The proposal includes a total of four different seed mixes, two of which were designed to improve treatment success in the different ecological sites and vegetation communities included within the burn. The other two seed mixes include one that was designed to protect the investment of the seedings, and the other was designed to protect the proposed Horse Hill ACEC. The burned area would be drill seeded in late fall or early winter to give seeds an opportunity to germinate without competition from undesirable vegetation. Prior to drill seeding, cultural resources that may be affected by the treatment will be identified and marked for\r\navoidance. Avoided sites will be seeded by hand with the seed mix used in the surrounding area to stabilize site surfaces and protect site locations.
Actual_Implementation: FY10 expense was for purchase of seed at BLM consolidated seed buy. FY11: See seeded species table below in Part 8.\r\nBLM FORCE account drill seeded 27,049 total acres using 4 tractors and 2 dozers, each pulling 3 drill sets. Standard rangeland drills without depth bands were used, provided by the Vale drill shop. Mix 1 was 12,722 acres and Mix 2 14,327 acres.\r\nDrill seeding began on 10/1/2011 and took approximately 6 weeks to complete. Ground conditions were predominately clear and dry with occasional rain storms occurring throughout the period.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Results
Drill Seeding Effectiveness
Objectives 1, 2, and 4 are being met; objective 3 is not being met.
1. Greater than 50% of basal gaps in drill rows are less than 100cm; therefore, the objective is being met (Table 8-3).
The percent of basal gaps less than 100cm between perennial grasses averaged 67.4% in Mix 1 plots (8 plots) and 83.4% in Mix 2 plots (7 plots) (Table 8-3).
2. As of 2012, plant communities representing both seed mixes had greater than a 20% increase in desirable perennial vegetation foliar cover and a 20% decrease in invasive annual grass foliar cover as compared to the control; therefore the objective was being met (Table 8-4). Foliar cover of both desirable perennial vegetation and introduced/invasive annual exotic species in the treatment areas decreased in 2013; however, treatment areas are maintaining the necessary percentages compared to the control area to meet the objective (Table 8-4).
3. The average percent of basal gaps greater than 50cm in treatment areas has not decreased 30% compared to control areas; therefore, the objective is not being met.
Mix 1 areas were meeting the objective and Mix 2 areas were nearly meeting in 2012 (Table 8-5). However, in 2013 the total average basal gaps between perennial plants greater than 50cm was only slightly below the control areas in 2013, not the 30% necessary to meet the objective (Table 8-5).
4. Diversity of desirable perennial grasses and forbs in the treatment area was greater than the control; therefore, the objective is being met.
Foliar cover data showed only a minor increase in diversity of perennial species in drill seeded areas over control areas (Table 8-3). However, 2013 Site Assessment information indicated that perennial grass, forb, and shrub diversity, as well as abundance, was slightly higher in treatment areas than indicated by Line Point Intercept data alone. Species present in the vicinity of the plots not captured in Line Point Intercept included Munro’s and goosefoot globemallow, desert parsley, and Townsend daisy. Shrubs such as Wyoming big sagebrush, gray (and/or green) rabbitbrush, shadscale saltbush, and bud sagebrush were present at many of the treatment plots, though the Line Point Intercept data may have only captured these species at one or two sites.
Conclusions
The drill seeding and grazing closure treatments have mostly been successful; specifically drill row basal gap, percent perennial species, and drill seeded grass vigor targets. Low spring moisture in 2012 and 2013 considerably reduced foliar cover of cheatgrass across the site. Similarly, dry conditions may have impacted seeded grasses to a small degree in terms of overall biomass and reproductive capability. However, these grassed are established and vigorous enough to persist into the future with proper livestock grazing management.

Plot T12 (see photos below) in Drill Mix 2 - Loamy had 40% perennial plant cover (primarily Siberian wheatgrass and needlegrass). Plot T14 in Drill Mix 2 – Loamy likely did not meet this objective in 2021. This plot lies within a bowl and two of the east/southeast-facing pinwheel plot lines are representative of the broader area. The third line is on a west-facing sandy slope with a different plant community. The east/southeast facing slope is predominantly Siberian wheatgrass with cheatgrass in the interspaces. Overall, the seeding is thin and patchy at this plot.

3. 30% decrease in basal gaps >50cm and as compared to a burned, untreated area. Conduct Basal Gap Intercept monitoring.
Basal gap was not measured but the objective of increasing desirable perennial plant foliar cover to outcompete exotic annual grass was likely met (see above under Objective 2) in 2021. In 2015, the Mix 1 area was meeting the objective (31% decrease in basal gaps) while Mix 2 was not (7% decrease) (Table 8-4). The total average basal gaps between perennial plants greater than 50cm was only slightly below the control areas in 2013, not the 30% necessary to meet the objective.

4. Increase the diversity of desirable grass and forb species, as compared to a burned, untreated control area. Conduct Line Point Intercept monitoring and Site Assessments.
In 2011, plot T01 had 10 native/seeded species and T07 had 4. While in 2021, 6 native/seeded species were found at both Mix 1 – Sandy plots. Four native/seeded species were noted at plot T12 (Mix 2 – Loamy) in 2011 which had 7 in 2021. Plot T14 (Mix 2) had 5 native/seeded species in 2011 compared with 12 in 2021. Overall, this objective has been met in both drill mixes.

Actual_Implementation:
To meet treatment objectives, the area was drill seeded by BLM
Force Account crews in December 2006 with Russian wildrye (Bozoisky), Siberian wheatgrass
(Vavilov), Sandberg’s bluegrass, and fourwing saltbush, using Standard Rangeland drills. (Note:
this area was also aerially seeded with a second seed mix.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Treatment Effectiveness: BLM monitoring crews established three monitoring plots in May
2007 within the drill and aerially seeded areas. Crews recorded plant species and density,
vegetative cover, and canopy gaps using quadrat, line-point intercept and gap intercept methods.
Treatment Results: It is too early to determine the success of the treatment, but there is a decent
stand of perennial grasses. No fourwing saltbush was recorded in the treatment area. Over 50%
of all perennial grasses had established seedheads, but this may include seeded and resprouting
vegetation.
 2007 monitoring recorded perennial grasses 33/m\xb2 and appeared to exhibit fair vigor with 53% producing seed heads (Figure 4). The vast majority of the perennial grasses recorded were small (basal area) individual native Sandberg bluegrass plants. Seeded perennial species were not recorded separately, but only accounted for a small portion of the total density recorded.  No fourwing saltbush was recorded or observed.
2008 monitoring recorded perennial grasses, primarily Sandberg bluegrass, 4.5/m\xb2, with good vigor as indicted by larger basal areas and the majority of plants producing seed heads. Dominant annuals were cheatgrass and Russian thistle, which were primarily growing in the drill rows (Figure 5). Seeded perennial grasses were recorded 0.5/m\xb2 and exhibited low vigor with 10 % producing seed heads.  No fourwing saltbush was recorded or observed.
2009 monitoring recorded all perennial grasses, which was almost entirely Sandberg bluegrass, at 11.6/m\xb2 (Figure 6).  Seeded perennial species were not recorded separately, but only accounted for a very small portion of the total density recorded.  A general evaluation of the site conducted in 2009, noted seeded perennial grasses as being in very low occurrence, exhibiting poor vigor and seed head production.  Fourwing saltbush was recorded in very low numbers on Plot 4 during a belt transect survey.  Based on third year monitoring (Plots 4, 5, & 6), the drill seeding treatment with no herbicide seedbed preparation was considered unsuccessful.

Wyoming big sagebrush and fourwing saltbush, which are valuable for soil protection and
wildlife habitat, particularly for wintering big game. Natural recovery of these native shrubs

native grasses and forbs.

noxious weed will spread rapidly as a result of the fire if its populations are not controlled.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Objectives and Results
1. >50% of seeded species basal gaps are =100cm. Conduct drill row basal gap intercept
monitoring to determine seedling establishment success (Only conducted in Year 1).
This method was only conducted in 2012 (the year following the seeding). Due to timing and
funding constraints drill row monitoring was not conducted in 2013. These metrics were also not
measured in 2014 due to 1) difficulty finding previous drill row plots and 2) questionable
selection of drill plot locations by monitoring crews in 2012. Therefore, no data specific to drill
rows are available, so overall treatment success is evaluated using objectives 2-4 and other site
assessment information.
2. 20% increase in foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation, and 20% decrease in
invasive exotic annual vegetation compared to control plot (burned and not drill seeded).
Conduct line point intercept monitoring to determine species cover/composition. (This
will only be conducted in years 2 and 3.)

In 2017, drill seeded plots had 21.3% greater foliar cover of desirable perennial vegetation than
the untreated plot outside of the exclosure. The average percent foliar cover of exotic annual
vegetation was 15.4% higher in that untreated plot compared to the drill seeded plots. Within the
exclosure, the drill seeded plot had a 21.9% higher average percent foliar cover for desirable
perennial vegetation than the non-drill seeded plot. The non-drill seeded plot also had 38%
higher average foliar cover of exotic annual vegetation (Figure 8-1, 8-2 and Table 8-2).
Since 2015, there was a 40% increase in percent foliar cover of exotic annual vegetation in the
non-drill seeded plot within the exclosure. There was a 6.7% increase in foliar cover of exotic
vegetation in the drill seeded plots. This objective has been met.
Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) comprises the majority of the foliar cover at the drill seeded
plots (41%) and the control drill seeded plot (51%). Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda)
comprises the majority of the foliar cover at the control plot that was not drill seeded within the
exclosure (50.7%) and the plot in the untreated area outside the exclosure (48%) (Figure 8-1, 8-2
and Table 8-2).

3. 30% decrease in perennial vegetation basal gaps >50cm compared to control plot.
Conduct basal gap intercept monitoring.
In 2017, basal gaps greater than 50 cm were higher in the non-drill seeded plots compared to the
drill seeded plots; this difference was only 6% therefore, this objective was not met in 2017
4. Qualitative increase in perennial grass and forb diversity compared to control area.
Conduct line point intercept monitoring and site assessments.
Site assessments and photos from 2017 indicate there was an increase in perennial forb diversity
in the drill seeded plots compared to the control plot.
Both the drill seeded and non-drill seeded plots within the exclosure (G4ZNC01 and G4ZNC02),
the untreated plot outside the exclosure (G4ZNNT01), and all of the drill seeded plots except
G4ZNT02, had three perennial grass species. Plot G4ZNT02 had two perennial grass species.
Siberian wheatgrass (Agropyron fragile) was dominant (40-100% composition) within all of the
drill seeded plots except for G4ZNT04 where it was subdominant (10-40% composition).
Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) was dominant at the untreated plot outside the exclosure
(G4ZNNT01) and subdominant at the drill seeded plots and at the non-drill seeded plot within
the exclosure. Bottlebrush squirreltail (Elymus elymoides) was subdominant at G4ZNNT01 and
drill seeded plot G4ZNT03, minor (2-10% composition) at the non-drill seeded plot within the
exclosure, and trace (<2%) at the drill seeded plot within the exclosure and drill seeded plots
G4ZNT01 and G4ZNT04. The drill seeded plots had more perennial forb diversity compared to
the drill seeded and non-drill seeded plots within the exclosure. Trace amounts of fleabane
(Erigeron) were noted at the drill seeded plot within the exclosure. Trace amounts of longleaf
phlox (Phlox longifolia) were found at drill seeded plots G4ZNT01 and G4ZNT03. Trace
amounts of larkspur (Delphinium sp.) were found at control plot G4ZNC01.
Comparing the non-drill seeded and drill seeded plots within the exclosure to the untreated plot
outside the exclosure, G4ZNC01 and G4ZNC02 both had subdominant amounts of Sandberg
bluegrass compared to G4ZNNT01 which had dominant. The percent cover of Siberian
wheatgrass was highest at the drill seeded plot within the exclosure (G4ZNC02).

Objectives: Reestablish Shrubs.
Planned_Implementation: Sagebrush will be aerially seeded at 1/4 lb. to the acre over\r\napproximately 12,000 acres of the eastern portion of the burned area in the\r\nwinter of 2000/2001 over the snowpack.
Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of aerial seeding 14,240 acres. Rate of application was approximately 0.9
pounds bulk seed per acre on the entire area and 11,497 acres which had previously been drill seeded.
The seed consisted of Wyoming Big Sage. The seed was applied to 50% snow covered ground, see
the attached map for the project location. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of Gooding,
10. Pilots for the seeding were Rod Thomas and Dale Thomas. The project was completed using a
helicopter and two sling type buckets. The project was started on 2/16/00 and completed on 2/17/00.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
On March 28, 2001, Paul Makela and myself visited these areas to check on early success of the seedings. 
The Brigham Point Seeding, following oust, appears to be coming in well. We found many grass seedlings in the drill rows at one location near the northeast edge of the area. Most of these were about 2 inches tall. 
The Mule Butte Seeding done in 1999 is greening up and still appears to be in fairly good order. It is still too early to tell if we have Secar coming in but the crested and tall wheatgrass types, as well as flax are doing well. We also found a fair number of Wyoming sagebrush seedlings as well as three-tip seedlings. This visit was done along a north-south road running through T5S R25E sections 24, 25, 35. Elk tracks were seen near Bear Trap Lava Tube. 
The Mule Butte Seeding done in 2000 after oust treatment was also looked at just north of the road and west of Crean1 Can Junction about 0.25 miles. We found only a few seedlings in the drill rows but as it is still early, a negative evaluation would be premature at this time. The "native" plants seeded here are expected to come in a bit slower than the exotics which were used on Brigham Point. 
The Whiskey Butte Seeding done in 1999 looks similar to the 1999 Mule Butte Seeding. We will need to wait a year or two before making a call on the Secar in this mix. We noted several sagebrush seedlings near the east central portion of the rehab where none were seeded. 
In the Rice Canyon Prescribed Burn area we looked at Rice (Lindy) Spring. There are numerous aspen sprouts up to 30" tall. We noted that approximately 1/3 of the tips were nipped, probably by deer. 
Also in the Rice Canyon area we looked at the old burn in the bottom of Rice Canyon which was burned, ousted and seeded/harrowed in 1999, 2000. Some seedlings were observed however they appear to be patchy. It was obvious where seed was spilled as there were hundreds of seedlings which at least tells us that they are growing. Most of the seedlings are quite small (\xbd to 1 \xbd " tall). From this area we drove eastward down the road at the south end of the burn area and found many seedlings along the draw/road. Near the southeast corner of the seeded area we looked at the southward facing slopes and found only a few seedlings but once again we saw many seedlings where seed was spilled. We also saw numerous seedlings at the extreme southeast corner at the road junction. Since we were involved with seeding this area, we know that this comer was seeded heavily and harrowed extensively. There is quite a bit of deer sign along the south end of this area and moderate to heavy use is occurring on about 1/3 of the established grasses within the burn. 
We also observed some cheatgrass seedlings throughout the ousted/seeded areas.

10/17/2001: The Mule Butte Fire was the Area's biggest in 1999, totaling 138,908 acres from the Craters of the Moon lava flow heading east 2/3 of the way to the BLM boundary. West of the Arco-Minidoka road little is left of unburned sage or skeletons. Towards the southeast, unburned islands become larger. This fire, especially across the southern half, was where I saw the strongest correlation between standing skeletons or close live sage and new seedlings. Within about 1 \xbd miles radius of Horse Butte are the biggest areas of totally unburned plants. 
The first seeding occurred in Jan. of 2000 on 73,800 acres. When that appeared not to be very successful, a smaller seeding of 64,000 acres across the northern 2/3 of the fire was repeated in Feb. of 2001. 
On Aug. 7-8 and 14-15, we read 103 plots on five transects, directly sampling 21.03 acres. We started using circular plots with a 33 foot radius and plot center spacing of 200 feet along a transect. That plot size has worked well with just one person. Toe thickness of ground cover slows you down a little, but still works well. Stretching one person to cover a 50 foot radius in any area not ousted is too much. Areas of thick cheatgrass slow you down to where the extra ground you cover in a larger plot isn't worth it. Our two-person crew worked well with the full chain radius spaced at 400 foot plot center intervals; and that method became our standard. 
We recorded seedlings in \xbd-inch height classes testing my theory that height results would show two recognizable peaks suggesting some success with the first years seeding. It appeared there were two swells, falling shorter of dramatic peaks, at about 3"-3 \xbd" and at 5"-6" heights. I can't make further conclusions since the majority of the evidence was all found on one transect. 
Over the summer while re-reading existing vegetation transects, we watched for seedlings but only observed any in two or three areas. Seedlings were un-evenly distributed, usually found in dips or drainages of the terrain and often in the vicinity of existing live shrubs. 
I have not been afraid to express my amazement at how fast vegetation has sprung up in those two years, granted that not all of it is desirable. The difference in plant growth, height and vigor in areas Ousted the previous year were also stark. I am not sure I believe it myself, but I saw very deep green, vigorous sage that was 14 "high but assumed to be two years old. Darwin Jeppsen had some interesting comments on his soil moisture observations in those treatments. 
Overall I think this fire had more areas of considerable seedling survival than others and how much to credit natural regeneration versus two years of treatment I can't say. In our meeting the question of any additional treatment areas was raised. At the time I said west of the Arco-Minidoka was the only area I could think of that might benefit but the final decision was not to pursue any further treatment. The more I think about it, the more I agree that two years was enough.

Monitoring Results:
FY07
Qualitative monitoring information was collected in FY07 during a reconnaissance of the
treatment area. Survey of the fire area showed poor germination of seeded species. Noxious
weeds were dominant on portions of the burn area. Spring moisture was well below normal
levels. Extended drought conditions may have had an effect on the germination of species.
Based upon the qualitative observations the aerial seeding at this point may be considered a
failure but a final determination should not be made until after the second growing season.
FY08
Qualitative monitoring information was collected in FY08 during reconnaissance of the
treatment area. There continues to be poor establishment of the seeded species. Noxious weeds
(knapweed and rush skeletonweed) are expanding within the area and are dominant in some
areas. With no evidence of seeded species, the treatment can be considered a failure at this point.
The area will be monitored again next year before making a final determination. The lack of
seed coverage and continued drought conditions appears to be the major contributors to the
failure. The rocky terrain makes it very difficult to apply a seed cover treatment.
FY09
Qualitative and quantitative monitoring information was collected in FY09. There continues to
be poor establishment of the seeded species. Noxious weeds are the major issue currently
impacting the fire area and will continue to be a focus of future treatments. The fire area is
stable in terms of soil stabilization. Recovery of existing native vegetation has contributed to the
soil stabilization. Cheatgrass is present (18% cover) but does not appear to be overly dominant.

The seed treatment will be considered a failure due to the lack of seeded species. Seed coverage
and drought conditions the first two growing seasons appear to be the major contributors to the
failure. The rocky terrain makes it very difficult to apply a seed cover treatment.

Site selection - Find an area representative of the treatment and soil mapping units. Establish a permanent witness post and describe the location so that another person could return to the area. Establish an imaginary transect line from the post by selecting a compass bearing which will traverse the sampling area. Avoid treatment edges, atypical microsites or crossing into very different range sites. Record transect azimuth in degrees magnetic. From the witness post, photograph a general view of the sampling area, with the skyline in the picture. The witness post may be included in the picture if desired. 
In following years, the transect can be re-sampled with another set of randomly-located plots. 
Seeding of forbs is probably not warranted in that the team has observed that native forbs such as Agoseris, globemallow, balsamroot and others were present prior to the fire and generally proliferate naturally after fire. We thus felt it more prudent to concentrate rehab efforts toward establishing ground cover and structure via seeding of native grasses and sagebrush. 
Vegetation sampling - Beginning at the witness post walk a random number of paces (not exceeding 30) along the transect and place the 9 .6-ft2 circular plot frame at your foot. Record the data. Repeat until 30 plots are recorded. Record, by number of individuals rooted or having > 50% of the basal area within the plot, the following:
seeded grasses by species 
seeded grasses, when species are not discernable 
seeded forbs by species 
shrub seedling resprout species dead shrub burned stumps, not by species live residual native bunch grasses or rhizomatous grasses by species 
dead native bunchgrass tufts, by species if possible, based on size of basal area and presence of nearby live species dead native bunchgrass tufts, when species are not discernable cheatgrass, by density

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
On June 11, 1996 I toured the native rehab area, particularly along the north edge and northeast comer. It is obvious (see pictures) that there is more cheatgrass in those areas that did not re-burn in 1995. It appears that the Bear Trap burn (1995) was somewhat beneficial because it removed the heavy cheatgrass thatch produced that spring due to above normal precipitation (18" for the year). I could not detect any mortality of grass seedlings due to the burn. 
Although the native rehab is not worthy of any awards (at least at this time) it is coming along as well as could be expected ( drilled much less than the 6 lbs. proposed). This year the native seedlings are becoming more apparent and a few set seed. In a few places the drill rows are quite apparent but in general you can't find long rows of seedlings. It is important to note that the exotic grass mix seeded in the NW comer of the burn did not do well at all. It is difficult to find any grass coming up ( other than cheatgrass) but the forbs ( flax and burnett) are present. 
The residual native grasses and forbs are growing well and appear to be undisturbed by drilling (see photos). Globemallow is prevalent, particularly in those areas not re-burned in 1995. 
I was able to find a few sagebrush seedlings but it appears that, for whatever reason, the aerial application of sage was a failure. We need another year or two to make a final call on this. The thick cheatgrass due to the high precipitation. the first growing season may have prevented establishment of the sage seedlings.

Objectives:
The objective of this treatment is to
establish a desirable perennial plant community that would help achieve a healthy, functioning rangeland and
significantly reduce the potential for spread invasive annual grasses and noxious weeds. The wildfire removed
the majority of existing plant cover making the burn area more susceptible to expansion of these plants. Natural
recovery of native vegetation is not possible given pre-burn vegetative conditions in the area.
Planned_Implementation:
The Chute allotment, the East, Substation, and Notch Butte pastures of the
Camp I allotment, the Milner Canal and Bacon pastures of the North Milner allotment, the North, Notch Butte,
and Substation pastures of the Notch Butte allotment, the Camp 2 pasture of the Star Lake allotment, the south
pasture of the Sand Butte allotment, and the East pasture of the Antelope allotment would be drill seeded in the fall of 2007. The proposed drill seeding area is approximately
28,390 acres. Approximately 80% or 22, 700 acres would actually be drill seeded in the area due to the presence
of rock outcrops and unburned islands. A standard rangeland drill and rubber tired tractor would be utilized for
the seeding treatment.
Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of drill seeding approximately 22,461 acres out of a 25,229 acre area within
the Red Bridge fire. Unburned islands of grass and sagebrush, numerous areas of rock, and areas
of archeological sites were the reason for reduction in acres completed. Seed was applied in dry
conditions at the beginning to wet ground later in the process. The contractor for the project was Richard Barney of Shoshone, Idaho.
Nine rangeland drills were used on approximately 18,462 acres. For the area near Shoshone and
State Highway 24, approximately 3,999 acres, BLM fire crew drill seeded using two rangeland
drills. The seed was premixed by Operations Staff with the assistance of fire crew. The project
was started on September 21 , 2007 and completed on November 19, 2007.

Red Bridge Contract Cost: $ 91,487.50 
Notch Butte Contract Cost: $ 28,954.20 
Total Cost: $ 120,441.70  

Seed Cost: $ 846,520.00
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Initial observations the first growing season showed fair to good germination of the seeded grasses and forbs throughout the treatment area. Quantitative monitoring plots were established in FY08.

Monitoring Results FY08
Preliminary monitoring was established on the Red Bridge fire. Qualitative observations
gathered at the established plots showed good establishment of drilled seeded grass and forb 
species. Bare ground across all plots was relatively high at 32% but this is within the range of
expectations the first growing season following a wildfire. Vegetation cover (canopy and basal)
averaged 39% across the plots. It is expected following the second growing season that the
overall cover will increase and bare ground will decrease once established perennial seedlings
gain in growth and vigor. Annual vegetation (cheatgrass) averaged 43 plants per square meter
across all plots.
Monitoring Results FY09
Quantitative and qualitative monitoring data was collected in FY09. Qualitative observations
showed continued good establishment of drill seeded grasses and forbs. Quantitative density
data shows that the seeded species (crested wheatgrass) are still below quantifiable objectives.
Bare ground cover across all plots was 17%, a reduction of almost 50% from the previous year.
Cheatgrass densities were also reduced by approximately 75%.

Monitoring Results FY10
Quantitative and qualitative monitoring data was collected in FY10. Qualitative observations
showed continued good establishment of drill seeded grasses and forbs. Quantitative density
data shows that the seeded grass species (Siberian and Snake River wheatgrass) are still slightly
below quantifiable objectives. Bare ground cover across all plots was 20%, a slight increase
from the previous year. Cheatgrass densities were also slightly increased.
A qualitative observation made within the treatment area was the amount of damage occurring to
vegetation from an outbreak of voles. The voles were significantly removing vegetation cover
across the treatment area including the monitoring plots. Seeded forbs were not recorded in the
plots probably as a result of vole damage. Overall seeded perennial grass was only slightly
below objectives. Native recovery of Sandberg's bluegrass was good.

Objectives:
The objective of this
treatment is to reestablish a desirable perennial plant community that more closely matches the
structural and species composition and diversity of the native plant community to help achieve a
healthy, functioning rangeland. Accelerating the rate of reestablishment of sagebrush is important
to maintaining the value of the area as big game winter range, sage grouse breeding and wintering
habitat. Sagebrush is also an important component of suitable habitat for a number of sensitive
sagebrush obligate species. The wildfire impacted existing sagebrush cover which would not
recover naturally without providing additional seed source.
Planned_Implementation:
Approximately 10,000 acres of the Red Bridge Fire wildfire
would be aerial seeded with a mixture of basin big sagebrush and Wyoming big sagebrush. The
seeding would be accomplished during the winter of 2007/2008. The burn area would be strip
seeded across the drill treatment area.
Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of aerial seeding 11,200 acres out of an area of 26,881 acres. This project
also included strip seeding Idaho State Land, approximately 1,478 acres, within the fire
perimeter and BLM boundaries for this contract. BLM provided the seed and contracting cost to
the Idaho Department of Fish & Game. Rate of application was approximately 1.00 pounds bulk
seed per acre. The seed consisted of 5,560 pounds of Wyoming and 5,680 pounds of Basin
Sagebrush which was mixed during the loading process. The seed was applied to snow covered
ground in strips from north to south on part of the project and east to west on the remainder. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc of
Gooding, ID. Pilot for the seeding was Rob Cantrell. The project was completed using one
helicopter and two sling type buckets. The project was started on 02/20108 and completed on
02/21/08.

Contract Cost: $ 20,000.00 
Seed Cost: $138,178.40
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
Quantitative monitoring plots were established in FY08. Initial monitoring did not measure any sagebrush seedlings on the established monitoring plots.

Monitoring Results FY08:
The sagebrush aerial seeding was not funded with 2881 BAR funds. The project was
implemented utilizing other BLM funds.
Sagebrush seedlings were not documented in quantitative plots. Qualitative observations will be
done in FY09 in addition to the quantitative plots to better document any seedling establishment
across the treated area.
Monitoring Results FY09
Sagebrush seedlings were not documented in quantitative monitoring plots in FY09. Qualitative
observations documented the presence of sagebrush seedlings across the treatment area.
Seedlings observed were scattered and relatively uncommon.
Monitoring Results FY10
Sagebrush seedlings again were not documented in quantitative monitoring plots in FY10.
Qualitative observations documented some presence of sagebrush seedlings across the treatment
area. Seedlings observed were scattered and relatively uncommon.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
FY 2017:
Monitoring plots were established during the summer of 2017. Cover, density, and belt transect
data were collected by ESR monitoring technicians (Tables 1-9). Data shows fair establishment
of perennial bunchgrasses. Yarrow establishment from the aerial seeding treatment was also
present. Cheatgrass competition was also high across the drill seeding areas.

FY 2018:
Monitoring data showed that nearly all of the seeded species either established in the plots or
were observed near the transects. The abnormal weather timing and duration over the winter
contributed to an abundance of invasive annuals and noxious weeds. These will continue to be
monitored in FY19. Seeded grasses have met the establishment objectives stated in the ESR
Plan.

In 2017, germination of drill seeded species was generally fair across the burn area. Fall
precipitation was abundant which allowed some of the drill seeding to germinate. Competition
with annual vegetation was moderate to high since cheatgrass germination also occurred in the
fall and growth continued into the spring.
Monitoring was completed in 2019 as part of a contract with the Institute for Applied Ecology.
Seeded species are establishing in measurable amounts, and are meeting the overall objectives of
the drill treatment. The moderate to high competition with annuals will continue to be an issue.
The use of a larger-scale herbicide application to reduce the invasive vegetation competition was
evaluated in 2019 after the growing season, and is recommended for long-term restoration in the
next few years.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
A primary objective of emergency stabilization is to “restore structure and function to fire damaged ecosystems.” Carbon sequestration is one of many ecological functions provided by healthy diverse plant communities.
Left untreated, the burned area will undoubtedly become dominated by cheatgrass and other highly flammable invasive annuals. The minimal root systems of these annuals accumulate little if any organic matter into the soil profile. Additionally, their flammability substantially increases fire frequency, thereby moving carbon from the soil profile into the atmosphere.
Conversely, reestablishing perennial vegetation within the burned area will have a positive benefit to climate change by the ability of these plants to sequester carbon. Deep rooted grasses in particular contribute substantial organic material into the soil profile both from their extensive root systems and recycle approximately \xbd of their root mass annually, thereby moving carbon from the atmosphere into the soil profile (providing long term carbon storage).
Reestablishing resilient perennial vegetation would also reduce fire frequency, reducing carbon emissions that would result if the site was allowed to become converted to a highly flammable exotic annual community.
In summary, the proposed seeding treatments would be expected to have a long-term indirect effect of decreased carbon emissions and increased soil carbon sequestration by potentially reducing high-intensity wildfires, slowing the rate of carbon turnover, and providing long-term below ground carbon storage.

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2018: First year results of ground seeding treatments showed variable effectiveness for re-establishing
a desirable herbaceous perennial plant community that more closely matches the structural and
species composition and diversity of the pre-burn native plant community (Figure 2, Table 7).
Most macroplots were dominated by invasive (tall tumblemustard [Sisymbrium altissimum],
cheatgrass [Bromus tectorum], redstem stork’s bill [Erodium cicutarium], herb Sophia
[Descuraina sophia], clasping pepperweed [Lepidium perfoliatum], curveseed butterwort
[Ceratocephala testiculata], kochia [Kochia scoparia], and bulbous bluegrass [Poa bulbosa]),
and/or noxious weed species (rush skeletonweed [Chondrilla juncea]) (Figure 3), while some
were dominated by high cover of recovering perennial grasses (Figure 4). Seeded perennial
grasses were recorded in all monitoring plots, and averaged 14 plants/m2, exceeding the
objective of 3 plants/m2 for this treatment. However, seeded forbs were observed on only two
monitoring plots, and averaged 0.07 plants/m2, while no bitterbrush seedlings were recorded;
thus the monitoring objectives for seeded forbs and shrubs were not met. Sites receiving both
aerial grass seeding and ground seeding had higher densities of seeded perennial grasses, with
14.8 plants/m2 versus 5.0 plants/m2 (however, this result is confounded by herbicide treatments
applied to the aerial grass seeding and not the drill seeding only sites). Identifying grass
seedlings to species, and separating seeded species from natural recruitment in the first year of
monitoring was sometimes difficult; however, Siberian wheatgrass, ‘Sherman’ big bluegrass, and
‘Craters’ bluegrass were most frequently observed in drill-seeding farrows (Tables 8 and 9;
Siberian wheatgrass and ‘Sherman’ big bluegrass were also seeded at much higher rates than any
other species). The next two years of monitoring will be essential for determining whether drill seeding
objectives are met, and better evaluating success of individual species.
Overall, line-point intercept monitoring recorded 61.7% canopy cover, 26.1% bare ground, and
6.8% basal cover (Table 7). Perennial grasses contributed an average of 24.3% canopy cover
while noxious species canopy averaged 7.6%, invasive annual forbs averaged 16.8% and
cheatgrass averaged 31.3% (Table 7). The majority of perennial grass cover came from resprouting
of existing grasses; dominated by the native Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) and
non-native previously seeded crested wheatgrass (Agropyron spicatum) and Siberian wheatgrass
(Agropyron fragile) (Figure 3). Recovery of existing perennial grasses has stabilized soils in
some areas of the burn, with good canopy and basal cover (Table 7), but areas dominated by
annual invasive species had high bare ground and low basal cover, and are highly susceptible to
wind and water erosion. Although canopy cover of sites dominated by invasive species was
relatively high at the time of measurement, these annual species do not provide perennial
protection from wind erosion, and their less extensive root systems do not anchor the soil.
Further, they provide very little in terms of basal cover, leaving soils highly susceptible to water
erosion.

2020: Summary
Drill seeding treatments
Three years post-treatment, the Shoestring ESR project area had almost 50 percent cover of perennial grass species, 7 percent of which came from seeded species. Seeded grass density averaged 2.3 plants/m2, which is not drastically below the 3 plants/m2 objective for drill treatment success.
Aerial grass and drill seed treatments were overwhelmingly dominated by Siberian wheatgrass, probably because of the dominance of this seed in the seed mixes and the establishment success of this stabilizing species. Other seeded grass species including Alkar tall wheatgrass, Sherman Sandberg bluegrass and Snake River wheatgrass, were present at low levels, establishing on a subset of ESR monitoring plots at lower densities and cover. These species were seeded at much lower rates than Siberian wheatgrass. Recovery of native perennial grasses including basin wildrye (Leymus cinereus), thickspike wheatgrass (Elymus lanceolatus), slender wheatgrass (Elymus trachycaulis), and needle-and-thread grass (Hesperostipa comata) were observed with variable rates of success across the monitoring area.
An established perennial grass community that covers bare ground and utilizes soil resources is better able to resist invasion by invasive and noxious species. Monitoring showed that invasive annual forbs did decline significantly with time and increased cover of perennial grasses on the Shoestring ESR project. Annual grass cover declined only slightly over the monitoring period. Areas that received aerial herbicide treatment in 2017 continued to have lower densities of invasive species than areas that had not been treated. Rush skeletonweed increased on the Shoestring ESR project, and new infestations of new noxious species (diffuse knapweed and scotch thistle) were observed. These small infestations should be a treatment priority before they become unmanageable.

Accelerating the rate of re-establishment of sagebrush is important to maintaining the value of the area as sage-grouse and big game habitat. The wildfire intensity impacted existing sagebrush cover which would not recover naturally without providing additional seed source.

Actual_Implementation:
This project consisted of aerial seeding 14,000 acres of BLM land.
This was a strip seeding of every other pass within the Shoestring
Fire. The total area of the project was 27,854 acres.
Rate of application was approximately 1.06 pounds bulk seed per
acre. The seed consisted of 9,720 pounds of Wyoming Sagebrush,
3,740 pounds of Basin Sagebrush, and 1400 pounds of Yarrow.
The seed was applied to bare muddy ground.
The contractor was Thomas Helicopters, Inc. of Gooding, ID. Pilot

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2018: A total of two big sagebrush and four yarrow seedlings were observed on three
monitoring belt transects for this fire in 2018, while none were observed on the remaining eight
transects. The average density of big sagebrush was 0.003 plants/m2 and 0.007 plants/m2 for
yarrow (Table 10). Sagebrush and yarrow seedlings were observed in the vicinity of a few
monitoring plots, but they were not observed to be common. Big sagebrush establishment and redominance
post-fire takes decades, but the low presence (well below 0.1 plants/m2 averaged
across all monitoring plots, and not common over the landscape in qualitative surveys) of
aerially seeded species indicates that aerial seeding on this fire has not yet met objectives.
Sagebrush recruitment was also observed in four cover/density plots for an average density of
0.08 plants/m2, which is closer to the seeding objective.

2020: Aerial sagebrush and forb seeding did not meet threshold densities for treatment success, thus this treatment did not meet objectives across the landscape. However, in some areas sagebrush and yarrow establishment was observed to be high enough where these species could be considered common, and treatment goals were met.
While sufficient cool temperatures were present in February 2018 when the treatment was applied to stimulate germination, seedling survival could have been enhanced by the longer duration of cool temperatures greater moisture availability in December and January. Sagebrush seeds are tiny and adversely impacted by competition, especially with aggressive non-native annual grasses. Seeding into dense stands of highly competitive plants is generally ineffective (Meyer and Warren 2015), and the large flush of non-native species in the spring of 2018 may have affected sagebrush recruitment success on this ESR project. Sagebrush recruitment from seed may also be limited on drier, rocky sites, or sites without microsite heterogeneity that traps snow (such as existing standing live or dead vegetation that is not too dense) (Schuman and Belden 2002, Meyer and Warren 2015). Seed banking of Wyoming and basin big sagebrush is thought to occur to a limited extent, with greater seed longevity if seeds are buried (Wijayrutne and Pyke 2009, 2012). Wyoming big sagebrush seedlings were observed on more monitoring plots in 2020 than in 2018, indicating that some seed banking of seeds from the initial seed application did occur.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
A primary objective of ES & BAR is to restore structure and function to fire damaged
ecosystems. Carbon sequestration is one of many ecological functions provided by healthy
diverse plant communities. Left untreated, the burned area would become dominated by
cheatgrass, invasive annuals, and noxious weeds. The minimal root systems of most all these
invasive annuals contribute little organic matter into the soil profile. Additionally, their
flammability substantially increases fire frequency, thereby moving carbon sequestered in the
standing vegetative material and herbaceous litter occurring on the site from being integrated
into the soil profile and releasing it into the atmosphere.
Conversely, re-establishing perennial vegetation through natural recovery, seeding treatments,
and noxious weed treatments within the burned area will have a positive benefit to climate
change by helping to assure the successful establishment and vigor of a diverse perennial plant
community leading to increased capacity for carbon sequestration. Deep-rooted grasses in
particular contribute substantial organic material into the soil profile. This is accomplished
through their extensive root systems which contributes and replaces approximately \xbd of their root mass annually, integrating the carbon constituent into the soil matrix leading to long-term
storage of carbon captured from the atmosphere.

In House: This project consisted of drill seeding an area of

Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2018: First year results of ground seeding treatments showed variable effectiveness for re-establishing
a desirable herbaceous perennial plant community that more closely matches the structural and
species composition and diversity of the pre-burn native plant community (Figure 2, Table 7).
Most macroplots were dominated by invasive (tall tumblemustard [Sisymbrium altissimum],
cheatgrass [Bromus tectorum], redstem stork’s bill [Erodium cicutarium], herb Sophia
[Descuraina sophia], clasping pepperweed [Lepidium perfoliatum], curveseed butterwort
[Ceratocephala testiculata], kochia [Kochia scoparia], and bulbous bluegrass [Poa bulbosa]),
and/or noxious weed species (rush skeletonweed [Chondrilla juncea]) (Figure 3), while some
were dominated by high cover of recovering perennial grasses (Figure 4). Seeded perennial
grasses were recorded in all monitoring plots, and averaged 14 plants/m2, exceeding the
objective of 3 plants/m2 for this treatment. However, seeded forbs were observed on only two
monitoring plots, and averaged 0.07 plants/m2, while no bitterbrush seedlings were recorded;
thus the monitoring objectives for seeded forbs and shrubs were not met. Sites receiving both
aerial grass seeding and ground seeding had higher densities of seeded perennial grasses, with
14.8 plants/m2 versus 5.0 plants/m2 (however, this result is confounded by herbicide treatments
applied to the aerial grass seeding and not the drill seeding only sites). Identifying grass
seedlings to species, and separating seeded species from natural recruitment in the first year of
monitoring was sometimes difficult; however, Siberian wheatgrass, ‘Sherman’ big bluegrass, and
‘Craters’ bluegrass were most frequently observed in drill-seeding farrows (Tables 8 and 9;
Siberian wheatgrass and ‘Sherman’ big bluegrass were also seeded at much higher rates than any
other species). The next two years of monitoring will be essential for determining whether drill seeding
objectives are met, and better evaluating success of individual species.
Overall, line-point intercept monitoring recorded 61.7% canopy cover, 26.1% bare ground, and
6.8% basal cover (Table 7). Perennial grasses contributed an average of 24.3% canopy cover
while noxious species canopy averaged 7.6%, invasive annual forbs averaged 16.8% and
cheatgrass averaged 31.3% (Table 7). The majority of perennial grass cover came from resprouting
of existing grasses; dominated by the native Sandberg bluegrass (Poa secunda) and
non-native previously seeded crested wheatgrass (Agropyron spicatum) and Siberian wheatgrass
(Agropyron fragile) (Figure 3). Recovery of existing perennial grasses has stabilized soils in
some areas of the burn, with good canopy and basal cover (Table 7), but areas dominated by
annual invasive species had high bare ground and low basal cover, and are highly susceptible to
wind and water erosion. Although canopy cover of sites dominated by invasive species was
relatively high at the time of measurement, these annual species do not provide perennial
protection from wind erosion, and their less extensive root systems do not anchor the soil.
Further, they provide very little in terms of basal cover, leaving soils highly susceptible to water
erosion.

Trt_Concerns_Desc:
A primary objective of ES & BAR is to restore structure and function to fire damaged
ecosystems. Carbon sequestration is one of many ecological functions provided by healthy
diverse plant communities. Left untreated, the burned area would become dominated by
cheatgrass, invasive annuals, and noxious weeds. The minimal root systems of most all these
invasive annuals contribute little organic matter into the soil profile. Additionally, their
flammability substantially increases fire frequency, thereby moving carbon sequestered in the
standing vegetative material and herbaceous litter occurring on the site from being integrated
into the soil profile and releasing it into the atmosphere.
Conversely, re-establishing perennial vegetation through natural recovery, seeding treatments,
and noxious weed treatments within the burned area will have a positive benefit to climate
change by helping to assure the successful establishment and vigor of a diverse perennial plant
community leading to increased capacity for carbon sequestration. Deep-rooted grasses in
particular contribute substantial organic material into the soil profile. This is accomplished
through their extensive root systems which contributes and replaces approximately \xbd of their root mass annually, integrating the carbon constituent into the soil matrix leading to long-term
storage of carbon captured from the atmosphere.

Establish Wyoming sagebrush on the fire area utilizing aerial seeding techniques.
For aerially seeded sagebrush – establish sagebrush densities of 0.1 plant/m2.
The amount of bare mineral soil (i.e. soil lacking cover of plants, litter, or biological soil
