Planned_Implementation: Unknown
Actual_Implementation: ES & BAR Fuels Rehab. Contractor was Thomas Helicopters, INC of Gooding ID.\r\nApproximately 920 acres were aerial seeded with Wyoming sagebrush. The project was completed in one day on December 15, 2010. ESR specialist monitored the activities and conditions.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results:
2011 Report: 3 ESR monitoring sites were established in the spring of 2011. Fuels monitoring crews collected cover and density data with photo plots during the late spring of 2011. Site visit was conducted by fire ecologist.
Data collected from the three belt transect monitoring sites show no occurrence of sagebrush. Subsequent monitoring in August and site visit by fire ecologist did not show any significant establishment of sagebrush. Additional time and monitoring will be required to determine the success of the project.
2013 Report: Cover and density data were collected in 2011 through 2013 by ESR monitoring technicians. Cheatgrass increased in cover and density between 2011 and 2012. Cheatgrass average cover
was 20.5% with 39.1 plants per square meter in 2011; 28.9% with 153.8 plants per square meter
in 2012; and 28.9% with 86.6 plants per square meter in 2013. Bare ground decreased from 52%
to 31.5%. Biological soil crust increased from 0% in 2011 to 2.2% in 2012. Biological crust
cover was not recorded in 2013.
Monitoring of belt transects in both 2011 and 2012 did not detect the presence of Wyoming big
sagebrush. However, sagebrush was detected in 2013 at a level that exceeds objectives for aerial
sagebrush seeding.
Fire ecologists conducted site visits in the vicinity of monitoring locations 1 and 3 at the end of
August 2011 and mid-August 2012. Site visits confirmed crested wheatgrass was dominant at
monitoring location 1 and cheatgrass was limited to small pockets scattered throughout the
crested wheatgrass.
Cheatgrass, tumblemustard, rush skeletonweed, and Russian thistle dominated the unseeded
areas around monitoring location 3 in 2011, but were less abundant in 2012 and 2013.
A site visit on July 11, 2013, documented good establishment of sagebrush seedlings along with
western yarrow. Low precipitation during May, June, and early July resulted in low grass stature
(including cheatgrass). However, forbs and sagebrush did not seem affected and may be
benefitting from reduced competition.\

RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS
It appears that some of the seeded species are establishing within the drill and aerial seeded
areas, even though they were not detected during monitoring. The most commonly detected
seeded plants were Wyoming big sagebrush, western yarrow, Munroe globemallow, Palmer’s
penstemon, and Siberian wheatgrass. Harsh site conditions (low precipitation and calcareous
soils) and competition may have impeded establishment of other seeded species.
Some of the drill seeded areas had previously been seeded to crested wheatgrass (see Part 12
below). This may not have been obvious due to dominance of the Wyoming big sagebrush
overstory. Crested wheatgrass appears to be resilient in the advent of subsequent fire and
continued to be present in the newly drill seeded communities. Diversification of these old
seedings was achieved, to some extent, by establishment of seeded sagebrush and forbs.

They observed crested wheatgrass was dominant in the SC001 area and cheatgrass was limited to small pockets scattered throughout the crested wheatgrass. Fire ecologists conducted site visits in the vicinity of monitoring locations 1 and 3 at the end of
August 2011 and mid-August 2012. Site visits confirmed crested wheatgrass was dominant at
monitoring location 1 and cheatgrass was limited to small pockets scattered throughout the
crested wheatgrass. Siberian wheatgrass was observed to interspersed with older crested
wheatgrass and Sandberg’s bluegrass plants, which were likely, at least in part, on-site native
plants.
Cheatgrass, tumblemustard, rush skeletonweed, and Russian thistle dominated the unseeded
areas around monitoring location 3 in 2011, but were less abundant in 2012 and 2013. Siberian
wheatgrass was observed to be common at monitoring location 3 and was interspersed with older
crested wheatgrass and Sandberg’s bluegrass plants. The drill seeded areas had less cheatgrass

The amount of bare mineral soil (lacking cover of plants, litter, or biological soil crust) is within 10% of what would be expected for the site,
•
Desirable herbaceous perennial plants are producing seed, and
•
Desirable perennial vegetation have developed extensive root and shoot systems to provide for soil stabilization and are sustainable under livestock grazing.
Actual_Implementation: This project consisted of aerial seeding 16,423 acres of the Jim Brown Fuels Project. The contractor was Thomas Helicopters out of Gooding, Idaho. Pilots for the seeding were Rod Thomas and Mike Cobb. The project was completed using two fixed wing aircraft. The grass and forb seed was premixed by ESR staff and Twin Falls fire employees. The project was started September 16, 2018 and completed on September 17, 2018.

Objectives:
The objective of the seeding treatment is to establish perennial-dominated plant communities within 3 years. The following grass, forb, and shrub density objectives are based on ecological site potential. The drill seed treatments would be considered successful if: The seeded grass, forb and shrub species reach densities of:
- 3 plants per square meter for grasses
- 0.30 plants per square meter for forbs
- 0.10 plants per square meter for shrubs (bitterbrush)
Planned_Implementation: Approximately 6,487 acres would be drill seeded with a grass/forb/bitterbrush mix.
Actual_Implementation: The project was partially completed in-house and partially through contract. The contractor did more than was anticipated because of their experience and equipment. Originally the project was expected to be 80% drillable, but Barneys did around 88%. Richard and Eric Barney were the contractor/operators. The in-house treatment used the Miller broadcast seeder pulled in-line with the Rangemaster drill distributing forb seeds.
Treatment_Effect_and_Results: 2023 monitoring data demonstrates the early establishment of desired vegetation. Additional monitoring and weed treatments are even more critical in 2024 to determine seeding success, need for follow-up treatments, and attain control of noxious weeds.
